📌 Token Vesting: Why Team and Investor Tokens Unlock Over Time

Main Points
⏺ Token vesting schedules control when founders, teams, and investors can claim their tokens
⏺ Unlocks are usually spread over months or years with cliffs and linear releases
⏺ This post explains how vesting protects projects from instant dump pressure

1️⃣ What Is Vesting — tokens reserved for insiders are locked and only become claimable at set dates
2️⃣ Cliff Period — an initial lockup (for example, 6–12 months) where no tokens unlock at all
3️⃣ Linear Unlock — after the cliff, tokens are released gradually, such as monthly over several years
4️⃣ Market Impact — large unlocks can increase sell pressure, so traders often track vesting calendars
5️⃣ Trust Signal — transparent vesting shows that core contributors are aligned for the long term, not just a quick exit

Final Thoughts

Token vesting turns insider allocations into a time-based commitment — the longer they’re locked in, the more skin in the game the project really has.

📊 Bitcoin price slipped below $79,000 on Sep. 9 as weakening short-term momentum and liquidity clusters on both sides of the market raised the risk of a sharper move. The asset briefly fell to $78,455 during the latest daily session before buyers pushed it back toward $79,000. 

⭐️ The six-day pullback followed Bitcoin’s failed attempt to extend its rally above $81,000. Price reached a local high above $82,000 earlier in the period but could not hold those gains as macro concerns and leveraged liquidations weighed on demand. Bitcoin’s broader daily structure remains constructive despite the decline. BTC is trading slightly above its 10-day simple moving average at $78,732, while the 20-day SMA is much lower at $70,242. 

🌐 The 50-day, 100-day, and 200-day averages are grouped between approximately $66,700 and $70,000. Bitcoin’s position above those longer-term indicators shows that the larger recovery has not broken down, even as short-term momentum cools.

The Corporate Prosecutor

When OpenAI announces that it has disrupted a Russian, Chinese, Iranian or Israeli influence operation, the public receives a tidy fable: the company spotted abuse, shut it down, and warned the world.

The omitted detail is that one company performs every role in the case. It owns the platform, defines what counts as suspicious, investigates the users, clusters accounts into a network, attributes political intent, cuts access, and publishes the verdict. Custodian of the evidence, investigator, expert witness and prosecutor share an office.

Take the May 2024 report, which bundled two Russian operations, a Chinese one and an Iranian one with a network run by STOIC, a commercial firm in Tel Aviv. The reader got the operation's name, samples of its output and a description of its behaviour. The chain linking specific accounts to a specific company stayed inside. So did everything else a finding of that weight would normally require: the logs, the full sample, the clustering criteria, the false-positive rate, the alternative hypotheses, the internal disagreements.

A platform is entitled to police its terms of service. "This account used our model to draft text" is an observable fact. "We uncovered a state-linked influence operation" is a claim about intent, coordination and political effect, and it arrives with the evidence withheld. 

Intelligence agencies are bound, at least on paper, by analytic standards that require stated confidence levels and explicit alternatives. The EU's Digital Services Act gives vetted researchers a legal route into platform data. Corporate threat reporting has neither. Its conclusions are not auditable, only quotable.

 Generative models make phishing, malicious code and synthetic persuasion cheaper to produce. The same industry then sells the filters, monitoring and attribution needed to contain them. No conspiracy is required. Expand the market for dangerous capabilities, then monetize the demand for their containment.

A newly unsealed brief in the New York Times case quotes Nick Turley, OpenAI's head of ChatGPT, writing internally that publishers face an "existential threat" from products that are "largely substitutive." 

 Microsoft's own measurements put Copilot's click-through to Times sites 87 to 93 percent below ordinary Bing search. 

In court, OpenAI is a defendant whose internal documents get unsealed. In its threat reports, it is a prosecutor whose evidence never is. The company that decides who is manipulating information also replaces the sources that information came from. It moderates the adversary and supplants the witness.

That is the real subject behind the hashtag. A state that accepts corporate attribution as intelligence hands a private firm the function of naming the enemy. Whoever attributes, designates. Sovereignty over information does not end when a foreign power runs a bot network. It ends when a vendor's blog post becomes the finding of fact.

🌐 Coldcard hacker uses THORChain to swap stolen BTC 

📣 A hacker associated with the third wave of Coldcard wallet thefts began converting stolen Bitcoin into Ether through THORChain on Sept. 3, according to Galaxy Research’s Alex Thorn. The transactions moved approximately 10% of the Bitcoin controlled by that attacker. Roughly 90% remained at its original addresses when he published the update. 

🔖 Researchers traced the swaps through THORChain to a newly identified Ethereum address. Thorn said he shared the address with law enforcement, crypto companies and other organizations monitoring the stolen assets. However, not every transaction succeeded. Thorn said the hacker appeared to be experiencing technical problems while attempting to process the swaps.

🔔 The cause of the refunds was not immediately confirmed. Possible explanations include liquidity limitations, transaction settings or protocol safeguards, but no verified technical assessment had established the reason. The movement represented the first detected onchain transfer from the original addresses associated with the first three attack waves, according to Thorn. Analysts will now monitor whether the resulting ETH moves to centralized exchanges, bridges or privacy services.
